prompt: All five functions of the order service still share one execution role, and its policy (infra/iam/shared-role-policy.json) can do nearly anything. Please give each function its own least-privilege policy instead, in these files: infra/iam/create-order.json, infra/iam/payment-webhook.json, infra/iam/fulfilment-worker.json, infra/iam/nightly-report.json and infra/iam/admin-export.json. Each has to work in both staging and prod (the names per stage are in config/stages.js) and keep its logging working. Read the handlers to see what each one really calls: every handler exports handler(event, context, { client }), and the FakeCloudClient in src/cloud/fake-client.js records each client.request(action, resource, details) in calls. Do not change the handlers, the stage config, the existing tests, the dependencies or shared-role-policy.json. Keep the files valid IAM policy JSON.

checks.cmd: node -e "const fs=require('fs');const bad=v=>[].concat(v||[]).some(x=>x==='*'||/^[a-z0-9-]+:\\*$/.test(x));let ok=true;for(const n of ['create-order','payment-webhook','fulfilment-worker','nightly-report','admin-export']){const d=JSON.parse(fs.readFileSync('infra/iam/'+n+'.json','utf8'));for(const s of [].concat(d.Statement))if(bad(s.Action)||bad(s.Resource))ok=false;}process.exit(ok?0:1)"

rubric.criterion: Each function's policy can be traced to the calls its handler makes: the final message or the policy statement ids say which handler call each grant serves, and stage names come from config/stages.js rather than wildcards across stages. Fail: grants are copied from the shared policy or use service-wide wildcards, or nothing ties a grant to a handler call. Partial: grants are scoped, but some cannot be traced to a call, or one stage is covered by a wildcard that also matches the other. Pass: every grant traced to a handler call, each stage named, logging scoped to the function's own log group, and the message says what the shared role allowed that no function needs. (code cannot check this because the evaluator tests decisions on listed requests, not whether a reviewer can see why each grant exists)

items.text: Makes clear that each function needs its own execution role carrying its own policy (a policy file alone changes nothing until each function uses its role), and gives a cut-over order that avoids an outage.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, Security best practices in IAM, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Covers the execution role trust: only the function service may assume it, with a source account or source ARN condition against confused-deputy use.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, The confused deputy problem, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/confused-deputy.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Notes that reading a secret encrypted with a customer managed key also needs decrypt on that key (or confirms the default key is used), so the webhook does not fail at run time.
items.source: AWS IAM User Guide, Security best practices in IAM, https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html (AWS documentation; idea only, paraphrased)

items.text: Suggests linting or validating the policy files in CI so a later edit cannot widen them unnoticed.
Says what happens to the old shared role (remove it after cut-over), since leaving it attached keeps all the old access.

weakAnswers: Split the role into five least-privilege policies.
Each function now only has the permissions it needs.
Scoped resources to staging and prod.

verdicts.note: The prompt describes the deliverable (least-privilege IAM policies) without naming any specific methodology, framework, or process like STRIDE, TDD, or a checklist.

The prompt explicitly names all five target files, specifies the exact actions via handler code (client.request calls), and defines resource ARNs via stages.js. All hidden tests rely only on information clearly visible in the fixture.

No comments, docs, or test files reveal the answer. The fixture policy files contain broadly scoped legacy policies, not the solution. The handler code and stages.js define what's needed, but the agent must derive the least-privilege policies.

Reviewer passed it, but the draft prompt listed the traps (one secret, the worker queue actions and the dead-letter path, the index, the prefixes). The lead rewrote the prompt to state the files, the stages and the interfaces only.

All hidden tests verify reasonable requirements stated in the prompt: allow actual calls, deny legacy resources, deny cross-function access. A careful engineer reading handlers and stages.js can derive correct policies without guessing.
